questions.stem: A replacement guarding system will cost $84,000 in four years. If funds can earn 5% annually, approximately how much should be invested today?
incorrectOptionExplanations: This rounds by subtracting four years of simple interest instead of discounting compound growth.
This applies an unsupported flat reduction rather than the present-value equation.
This compounds the future cost forward instead of discounting it to today.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 20, future and present value of money, pp. 495-499

questions.stem: A company places $30,000 in a safety-capital reserve earning 4% annually. What is the approximate value after five years?
incorrectOptionExplanations: This adds only one year of interest to the principal.
This uses simple interest and ignores annual compounding.
This applies a 50% increase that is unsupported by the stated rate and period.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 20, compound interest and future value, pp. 496-499

questions.stem: A short-term safety project borrows $50,000 for 18 months at 6% simple annual interest. How much interest will accrue?
incorrectOptionExplanations: This calculates only one year of interest instead of 1.5 years.
This treats the 18-month period as two full years.
This is the principal plus interest, not the interest amount requested.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)

questions.stem: A machine-guarding upgrade costs $80,000 and produces documented annual benefits of $112,000. Using net benefit divided by cost, what is the first-year ROI?
incorrectOptionExplanations: This divides the net benefit by the gross benefit rather than by the investment cost.
This divides cost by benefit and reports the inverse relationship.
This reports gross benefit divided by cost without subtracting the investment.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 20, engineering economic comparisons and return on investment, pp. 495-504

questions.stem: A $180,000 ventilation improvement is expected to save $45,000 per year in operating and loss costs. Ignoring discounting, what is the payback period?
options: 4 years
2.5 years
3 years
5 years
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Payback period = initial cost/annual savings = 180,000/45,000 = 4 years.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This divides annual savings by investment instead of investment by annual savings.
This assumes $60,000 annual savings, which is not stated.
This assumes only $36,000 annual savings and overstates the period.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 20, economic comparison of alternatives, pp. 495-504

questions.stem: A proposed control costs $150,000 and is expected to produce $270,000 in monetized benefits. What is the benefit-cost ratio?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Benefit-cost ratio = benefits/costs = 270,000/150,000 = 1.8. A value above 1 indicates benefits exceed costs under the assumptions.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This is the inverse cost-to-benefit ratio.
This subtracts cost from benefit and then divides by cost.
This divides the net benefit by the total benefit.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 20, engineering economics and economic analysis, pp. 495-504

questions.stem: Two controls produce the same verified risk reduction. Control A costs $90,000 and Control B costs $125,000. Which economic comparison is most appropriate for selecting between them?
options: Select the control with the largest capital cost
Compare only each control annual maintenance cost
Compare cost per equivalent unit of risk reduction
Choose the control with the longest implementation schedule
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: When alternatives achieve the same outcome, cost-effectiveness compares the cost required to achieve that common unit of benefit or risk reduction.
incorrectOptionExplanations: A higher cost does not establish greater effectiveness when the risk reduction is already equivalent.
Maintenance is only one cost component and cannot replace a full cost-effectiveness comparison.
Schedule length is a project constraint, not the economic measure requested.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 20, cost-effectiveness and economic decision methods, pp. 495-504

questions.stem: During installation of a fall-protection system, several departments request unrelated lighting and flooring upgrades. What should the project manager do first?
options: Add all requests immediately because they improve safety
Reject every request because scope can never change
Allow each department to direct the contractor independently
Evaluate the requests through formal change control against the approved scope
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Formal change control protects the approved objective while allowing justified changes to be evaluated for impact and authorization.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Potentially useful work still requires evaluation for cost, schedule, risk, and authority before inclusion.
Project scope may change, but changes should be controlled and documented.
Independent direction creates conflicting requirements, uncontrolled cost, and accountability gaps.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 20 and accompanying project-management homework, project scope and change control

questions.stem: A project schedule shows that delaying Task C by one day delays the final completion date, while Task D has three days of float. What does this indicate?
options: Task C is on the critical path
Task D is on the critical path
Both tasks have equal schedule priority
Neither task affects project completion
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: A critical-path task has no available float; a delay directly delays the project finish unless corrective action changes the schedule.
incorrectOptionExplanations: A task with three days of float can slip within that allowance without necessarily moving the finish date.
The stated float values show the tasks do not have equal schedule sensitivity.
The scenario explicitly states that delaying Task C moves project completion.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 20 and project-management homework, scheduling and project-control concepts

questions.stem: Which project-management display is best for showing activities as horizontal bars against calendar time, including planned start and finish dates?
options: Fault tree
Gantt chart
Risk matrix
Fishbone diagram
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: A Gantt chart displays project activities across a time axis, making duration, overlap, milestones, and progress visible.
incorrectOptionExplanations: A fault tree analyzes combinations of failures leading to an undesired event.
A risk matrix ranks likelihood and consequence rather than showing a calendar schedule.
A fishbone diagram organizes potential causes and does not display task timing.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 20 project-management homework, scheduling tools

questions.stem: A safety-system implementation repeatedly stalls because no one has final decision authority. Which RACI role should be assigned to one person for each deliverable?
options: Consulted
Informed
Accountable
Responsible only
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: In a RACI model, the accountable person owns the outcome and final approval; that role should be unambiguous for each deliverable.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Consulted parties provide input but do not own final approval.
Informed parties receive updates after or during decisions but do not own them.
Several people may be responsible for performing work, while one person should remain accountable for the result.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Project-management principles aligned to Yates Chapter 20 course homework

questions.stem: A critical ventilation component has a moderate probability of arriving late and would delay startup by six weeks. Which response best represents risk mitigation?
options: Ignore the risk until the original supplier misses the date
Transfer all project responsibility to the installation contractor
Remove the component from the design without technical review
Order early and prequalify an alternate supplier before the delivery deadline
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Mitigation reduces probability or impact before the event by adding schedule protection and a credible alternate source.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Waiting until the risk occurs is passive acceptance, not proactive mitigation.
Contract language may transfer some financial exposure but does not remove schedule and safety consequences.
Deleting a required component could create an uncontrolled technical and safety risk.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Yates Chapter 20 project-management homework, project risk mitigation
